name: Obadiah
author: The book is credited to Obadiah, whose name means 'servant of the Lord'. He was a prophet, someone who brought God's messages to the people, but nothing else is known about his family, hometown or life. Several other Old Testament figures share the name, though there is no good reason to link him with any of them.
audience: The message is addressed to Edom, a neighbouring nation descended from Esau, Jacob's brother. Its real first hearers, however, were the people of Judah, many of them grieving or displaced after Jerusalem had been attacked and plundered while the Edomites looked on and joined in.
era: Most scholars connect the book to the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC, when Edom sided with the invaders and took advantage of Judah's collapse. Some instead date it earlier, to around 845 BC, when Philistines and Arabs raided Jerusalem during King Jehoram's reign. Either way, Israel and Edom had a long history of bitter rivalry stretching back centuries, despite their shared ancestry.

notes.1:1: Edom's homeland lay in the rugged red-rock mountains south-east of the Dead Sea, where cliff-top settlements made its people feel safe from attack. This passage closely parallels Jeremiah 49.
notes.1:10: This section is widely linked to Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC; Psalm 137 also remembers Edomites cheering the city's destruction.

flags.problem: This describes the first hearers as grieving or displaced after Jerusalem's plunder, with Edom joining in. That presents the 586 BC setting as settled fact. The era section rightly says the date is disputed, and that some place the book around 845 BC, when the circumstances were quite different.
flags.suggestion: Make it conditional to match the era section, e.g. 'the people of Judah, stung by Edom's behaviour when Jerusalem was attacked and plundered (see The era for when this may have been)', and drop 'grieving or displaced'.
